title: 3-Read Friday #14: Variation Theory, Phone Bans, and CPD
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #14 curates three posts on classroom technique, technology policy, and professional development. Dylan Kane, in a follow-up to an earlier Variation Theory post Barton had shared, gives a concrete classroom example of using a carefully sequenced set of rounding examples on a mini-whiteboard to support a struggling student. Daisy Christodoulou uses the UK government's announcement of school phone bans to reflect more broadly on how societies decide which new technologies are on "the right side of history," arguing today's confident predictions about mobile phones may look as dated as smoking once did. Paul Cline challenges the assumption that good CPD must always introduce something new, arguing that refining and doing more of what teachers already know is often the more powerful lever. Barton connects the three as different reminders that thoughtful application -- of examples, of technology judgments, of professional learning -- matters more than novelty.
points: Dylan Kane's rounding sequence (3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6...) shows Variation Theory applied live with a single struggling student, changing one digit at a time to isolate cause and effect.

Daisy Christodoulou compares confident predictions about mobile phones to the FTX/Larry David "right side of history" advertising campaign, warning that being on-trend today is no guarantee of being right in ten years.

Paul Cline argues CPD framed as "nothing new" -- refining retrieval practice, modelling, or examples the teacher already uses -- can be more valuable than introducing new initiatives teachers won't sustain.

Barton's pairing of a granular classroom technique with a sweeping technology-policy essay shows the newsletter's range: the same issue can zoom into one student's whiteboard and out to a national policy debate.
quotes: What I love about Dylan’s post is that he describes in detail how he used a fundamental principle of Variation Theory to support a student who was struggling with rounding, armed with nothing more than a mini-whiteboard and a lovely sequence of examples.
So, who better than to shed some new light on the current debate surrounding mobile phone use in schools?
I think we will look back on the way mobile phones are used now the way we look back on how people smoked cigarettes in the past.
As someone who is fortunate to deliver lots of CPD, I had neckache as I was nodding so much throughout Paul’s post.
Paul instead challenges teachers to ask themselves: Can I do it more? and Can I do it better?
